In [[set theory]], a '''Jónsson cardinal''', named after [[Bjarni Jónsson]], is a certain kind of [[large cardinal]] number.

An [[uncountable set|uncountable]] [[cardinal number]] <math>\kappa</math> is said to be '''''Jónsson''''' if for every function <math>f : [\kappa]^{<\omega} \to \kappa</math> there is a set <math>H</math> of order-type <math>\kappa</math>, such that for each <math>n</math>, <math>f</math> restricted to <math>n</math>-element subsets of <math>H</math> omits at least one value in <math>\kappa</math>.

Every [[Rowbottom cardinal]] is Jónsson. By a theorem of Kleinberg, the theories ZFC + “there is a [[Rowbottom cardinal]]” and ZFC + “there is a Jónsson cardinal” are equiconsistent. Mitchell proved, with the help of the Dodd-Jensen [[core model]], that the consistency of the existence of a Jónsson cardinal implies the consistency of the existence of a [[Ramsey cardinal]], so that the existence of Jónsson cardinals and the existence of Ramsey cardinals are equiconsistent.{{sfnp|Mitchell|1999}}

In general, Jónsson cardinals need not be large cardinals in the usual sense: they can be [[singular cardinal|singular]]. But the existence of a singular Jónsson cardinal is equiconsistent to the existence of a [[measurable cardinal]]. Using the [[axiom of choice]], a lot of small cardinals (the <math>\aleph_n</math>, for instance) can be proved to be not Jónsson. Results like this need the axiom of choice, however: The [[axiom of determinacy]] does imply that for every positive natural number <math>n</math>, the cardinal <math>\aleph_n</math> is Jónsson.

A '''Jónsson algebra''' is an algebra with no proper subalgebras of the same cardinality. (They are unrelated to [[Jónsson–Tarski algebra]]s.) Here an algebra means
a model for a language with a countable number of function symbols, in other words a set with a countable number of functions from finite products of the set to itself. A cardinal is a Jónsson cardinal if and only if there are no Jónsson algebras of that cardinality. The existence of [[Jónsson function]]s shows that if algebras are allowed to have infinitary operations, then there are no analogues of Jónsson cardinals.
